messages.author: b08b7e19b674e717
messages.subject: mixedmirt() related query
parts:
Hi Phil,

I have a question on mixedmirt() function. Based on the function description and examples that you have provided, I understand that person-level and item-level covariate terms can be entered into a mirt model, using the 'covdata' and 'itemdesign' dataframes, respectively. My question is that is it possible to specify person-level covariate terms that only affect a specific set of items (i.e., interaction terms between covariates and items) ? Currently, all items seem to include the effects of covariate terms with an interpretation that the covariates basically change the underlying latent traits being measured in the subjects. An application of this kind of specification is in performing a confirmatory MIRT modeling of data, where certain items are found to illustrate differential item functioning for some subject groups (such as gender or race). The covariate-item interaction terms will then basically measure difference in item difficulties between patient groups (in case of uniform DIF). 

I am aware that parameter estimation in this scenario can be performed using the 'multipleGroup' function. However, I am trying to use mirt package for a problem that involves longitudinal modeling of subjects' responses, which will require use of random covariate terms, as in 'mixedmirt' function. 

I would appreciate your help in this regard.

Thanks,
Nishant

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt() related query
parts:
Hi Nishant,

This is an interesting question, but I'm having trouble understanding what it would look like. Usually when you include person-level covariates these effects are in some way time invariant and therefore should affect all item responses (hence, form the regression θ = β X + ε, where θ is simply being modeled by other relevant fixed factors). So its difficult for me to understand why some person-level covariates would be non-existent across items. Could you perhaps provide an example of this?

I think the interpretation of item blocks interacting with person level covariates makes sense for the most part, where, say, the first n items form block 1, while the next k form block 2, then the interaction of person level covariates with block design (or individual items, if you go that way to form as many blocks as items) would signify how the items modulate the person level variables across the item design blocks....but this would 'remove' them per say, just modify their influence for different blocks and require an extra coefficient to be estimated. However, I think this is probably the effect you are going for anyway. Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.author: b08b7e19b674e717
messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt() related query
parts:
Hi Phil,

Thanks for your reply. Yes, you are correct that if there are person-level covariates that affect the underlying latent traits (θ), then all items should illustrate the effects of these covariate terms. However, I was trying to point towards a slightly different scenario wherein, the covariate terms actually affect the item characteristic curves of certain items rather than the latent traits. I am not sure if statistical modeling theory has been developed for such scenarios. As an example, let us consider a test designed for measuring memory recall in subjects. Now, certain items on the test turn out to be biased because subjects belonging to a particular occupation are exposed to similar contents (as in the biased items) in everyday life and, therefore, they illustrate much higher likelihood of responding to those items correctly. During IRT modeling, this effect can be easily detected using DIF and, traditionally, such items may be removed from the test. If item deletion is not an option (such as in the case of retrospective analysis of tests that were not analyzed with IRT during design), separate IRT modeling of subject groups can also be performed. However, this would result in different item and subject scales. Therefore, it would be quite meaningful to have a methodology to be able to incorporate DIF effects within the model so that all subjects are measured on the same scale. For example, if DIF is uniform in nature, then the item response function (IRF) can contain a fixed intercept effect to adjust the difficulty parameter for certain subject groups. In mathematical terms, this model will look as containing person-covariate terms in IRFs of only some items in the test. Such covariate terms will basically account for changes in IRF functions due to DIF across subject groups. However, if there are person-level covariate terms across all items in the test, that will account for factors that may affect the underlying latent traits - thereby, affecting all items in the test. Does this make any sense ?

Thanks,
Nishant

parts: On Thu, Jul 31, 2014 at 11:04 AM, Nishant Verma <nisha...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Phil,

Thanks for your reply. Yes, you are correct that if there are person-level covariates that affect the underlying latent traits (θ), then all items should illustrate the effects of these covariate terms. However, I was trying to point towards a slightly different scenario wherein, the covariate terms actually affect the item characteristic curves of certain items rather than the latent traits. I am not sure if statistical modeling theory has been developed for such scenarios. As an example, let us consider a test designed for measuring memory recall in subjects. Now, certain items on the test turn out to be biased because subjects belonging to a particular occupation are exposed to similar contents (as in the biased items) in everyday life and, therefore, they illustrate much higher likelihood of responding to those items correctly. During IRT modeling, this effect can be easily detected using DIF and, traditionally, such items may be removed from the test. If item deletion is not an option (such as in the case of retrospective analysis of tests that were not analyzed with IRT during design), separate IRT modeling of subject groups can also be performed. However, this would result in different item and subject scales. Therefore, it would be quite meaningful to have a methodology to be able to incorporate DIF effects within the model so that all subjects are measured on the same scale. For example, if DIF is uniform in nature, then the item response function (IRF) can contain a fixed intercept effect to adjust the difficulty parameter for certain subject groups.

But this is exactly what an interaction of group membership by item does, create an extra intercept that only affects one group and not the other by design. So in short, yes this is possible to do in mixedmirt(), just specify a design matrix for items which you believe are systematically easier/more difficult given the group membership, and form an interaction term between the two in the model formula. Actually, if your model is a Rasch type this could also be done with lme4, so it might be good to check out the literature on how to do this with generalized mixed effects models as well (at least conceptually it will help).

In mathematical terms, this model will look as containing person-covariate terms in IRFs of only some items in the test. Such covariate terms will basically account for changes in IRF functions due to DIF across subject groups. However, if there are person-level covariate terms across all items in the test, that will account for factors that may affect the underlying latent traits - thereby, affecting all items in the test. Does this make any sense ?

Yes it does, and it really does sound like a simple uniform DIF test for each item of interest (or modeled all at once). The key is to form the appropriate itemdesign data.frame and have the specific terms interact with the group membership. You'll need a column for each item of interest in the data.frame, but otherwise it should be easy to construct. Cheers.

Phil

Thanks,
Nishant

parts:
Thanks Phil ! I was able to figure out the design matrices and successfully model interactions between items and person covariates. I had one more question - I was going through the examples that you provided with the mixedmirt() function. Specifically, this one:

#random slopes with fixed intercepts (suppressed correlation)
rmod3 <- mixedmirt(data, covdata, 1, fixed = ~ 0 + items, random = ~ -1 + pseudoIQ|group)
summary(rmod3)
(eff <- randef(rmod3))

eff$pseudoIQ contains 2 columns of 'pseudoIQ' and 'group'. 

> eff$pseudoIQ
     pseudoIQ       group
G1 1.57032254 -0.05721247
G2 0.05408288  0.03605942
G3 1.08146330 -0.01116472

According to my understanding, this example is trying to include a random slope effect (random over the 3 groups) for pseudoIQ predictor in the model i.e., θ = β X + a*(pseudoIQ)+ ε, where a ~ N(0, \sigma). So, the 1st column in the output represents the 3 random slopes associated with the pseudoIQ predictor. I am not able to understand what the other column of 'group' contains. Does it mean that besides estimating random slope for pseudoIQ, it also estimates random intercepts of groups ? If that is the case, is there a way to suppress the calculation of random intercepts and just calculate the random slopes ? I tried to look at the matrix designs (using return.design = TRUE) to understand this but the 'Z' design matrix always turns out to be NaN. Can you please throw some light on this ?

Thanks,
Nishant

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt() related query
parts:
Random slopes are always within the defined groups given by the | operator. This is true of other packages like nlme and lme4 since in order to define random variation of slopes the grouping factor has to be defined as well as the group intercept variation (the second column). So if you did something like this in lme4 with the syntax

dv ~ 0 _+ (cov | group) 

and predicted the random effects with randef() you would get both a slope and intercept within the levels defined by group. The first example in the lme4::lmer() function shows the same effect. Cheers.

Phil
